title: WOULD YOU STILL CALL IT LOVE IF SEX WERE REMOVED FROM THE RELATIONSHIP?
paragraphs: WOULD YOU STILL CALL IT LOVE IF SEX WERE REMOVED FROM THE RELATIONSHIP?
If physical intimacy disappeared tomorrow, would they still choose your heart—or would you finally discover that your body was the only thing keeping them close?
There is a question that could make some relationships stronger, expose others, and bring a few people to tears before they even finish reading it.
If sex were completely removed from your relationship, what would actually remain?
Not for one night.
Not for a week.
Imagine that, for reasons beyond your control, physical intimacy was no longer possible.
Would the conversations still be meaningful?
Would the laughter still come naturally?
Would the tenderness remain when there was nothing physical to gain?
Would that person still reach for your hand, pray beside you, protect your dignity, listen to your fears, and choose you when loving you required sacrifice instead of satisfaction?
Or would the relationship slowly become a room filled with two strangers who suddenly realized they had mistaken physical chemistry for emotional intimacy?
That question is uncomfortable.
Perhaps because somewhere deep inside, some people already know the answer.
And perhaps because others are terrified to find out.
But before anyone misunderstands what follows, we need to establish something important.
Sex is not dirty. Sex is not the enemy. And the Bible does not teach that genuine romantic love must exist without sexual desire.

God created human beings with bodies, affection, attraction, and the capacity for marital intimacy. Within marriage, sexual union is a beautiful gift meant to express mutual love, faithfulness, and covenantal belonging.
The problem begins when something God designed to express love becomes the primary condition for receiving it.
When affection disappears unless access is granted.
When tenderness becomes a transaction.
When someone says, "I love you," but their behavior quietly adds, "As long as you keep giving me what I want."
And sometimes, the most painful discovery is not that somebody stopped loving you.
It is realizing that what they called love may never have grown beyond desire.
There is a difference.
A heartbreaking difference.
And Scripture refuses to let us pretend otherwise.
In 1 Corinthians 13:4–7, the apostle Paul gives us one of the most recognizable descriptions of love ever written.
But familiarity can make us miss how confrontational those words really are.
Paul writes in Greek:
Ἡ ἀγάπη μακροθυμεῖ, χρηστεύεται ἡ ἀγάπη.
Hē agapē makrothymei, chrēsteuetai hē agapē.
"Love is patient, love is kind."
The word ἀγάπη (agapē) refers here to love characterized by a commitment to another person's good.
The word μακροθυμεῖ (makrothymei) carries the sense of being patient or long-suffering.
And χρηστεύεται (chrēsteuetai) describes acting with kindness.
Notice what Paul does not say.
Love is patient until your desires are frustrated.
Love is kind until somebody establishes a boundary.
Love remains faithful only while the relationship is physically satisfying.
No.
Paul continues:
οὐ ζητεῖ τὰ ἑαυτῆς
Ou zētei ta heautēs.
Love "does not insist on its own way" (1 Corinthians 13:5, ESV).
That phrase should make every person who claims to love somebody examine their heart.
Because love does not turn another person's body into a debt that must be collected.
Love does not punish someone emotionally for saying no.
Love does not use guilt, spiritual language, withdrawal, or threats to obtain sexual access.
And love does not confuse another person's willingness to surrender their boundaries with proof of devotion.
A person who truly loves you should care about what happens to your soul, not merely what happens between your bodies.
Now, we must be careful with the context.
Paul was not originally writing a modern relationship compatibility test.

He was addressing a church divided by pride, rivalry, spiritual competition, and self-centered behavior. First Corinthians 13 sits within his teaching about spiritual gifts and the need for believers to build one another up.
His point is that even impressive spiritual activity becomes empty without love.
But those principles absolutely challenge how Christians treat people in romantic relationships and marriages.
Because if love must be patient, kind, truthful, and unselfish among believers, how could it suddenly become demanding, manipulative, and self-serving behind closed doors?
Think about that.
Some people are extraordinarily gentle in public.
They quote Scripture.
They worship passionately.
They call their partner a blessing from God.
But privately, when physical affection is refused, their personality changes.
Their warmth disappears.
Their patience evaporates.
Their words become weapons.
And the person they claim to cherish begins feeling that peace in the relationship depends on keeping them sexually satisfied.
That is not the sacrificial love Paul describes.
And no amount of Christian vocabulary can make coercion holy.
Maybe somebody reading this knows exactly what that feels like.
You learned to say yes when your heart wanted to say no.
You became afraid that setting boundaries would cost you the relationship.
You confused being desired with being valued.
And somewhere along the way, you started believing that if you could keep someone physically interested, perhaps they would eventually learn to love the rest of you.
Your mind.
Your convictions.
Your wounds.
Your dreams.
Your relationship with Jesus.
But hear this carefully.
You should never have to surrender your dignity to prove that you are worthy of love.
You are not a body someone is entitled to use.
You are a human being created in the image of God.
Genesis 1:27 grounds human dignity in God's creation of humanity in His image.
Your worth did not begin when somebody found you attractive.
And it does not disappear when somebody stops desiring you.
You were valuable before anyone wanted to date you.
Before anyone kissed you.
Before anyone called you beautiful.
Before anyone promised forever.
And if someone walks away because you refuse to violate your convictions, their departure does not erase your value.
Sometimes the loss of a relationship reveals a painful truth.
But it can also open the door to a healthier future.
Still, this conversation is not only for unmarried couples.
It reaches into marriage, too.
Because marriage brings a different responsibility and a deeper covenant.
Scripture celebrates marital intimacy.
Genesis 2:24 describes husband and wife becoming "one flesh."
Proverbs 5:18–19 celebrates delight in one's spouse.
The Song of Songs openly portrays marital desire as something beautiful rather than shameful.
And 1 Corinthians 7:3–5 teaches mutual marital responsibility, including sexual intimacy, while recognizing circumstances in which spouses may mutually agree to abstain for a time.
But none of these passages gives one spouse permission to coerce, threaten, or disregard the other's well-being.
Paul's language in 1 Corinthians 7 emphasizes mutuality, not unilateral domination.
Marriage calls two people into covenantal love.
It does not turn either person into property.
And this becomes painfully important when life changes.
Imagine a husband sitting beside his wife after a serious medical diagnosis.
The treatments have exhausted her.
Her body is changing.
Her energy is gone.
The intimacy they once enjoyed has become difficult, perhaps impossible for a season.
Now imagine him looking at her, not with resentment, but with tenderness.
He brings her water.
He remembers her medication.
He sits beside her when she cries.
He tells her she is beautiful even when she struggles to recognize herself.
He holds her hand through another appointment.
And when she apologizes for not being the wife she used to be, he quietly reminds her that his vows were never limited to the healthy version of her.
That is not the absence of love.
That is love being revealed under pressure.
Now reverse the picture.
A husband suffers an injury.
He loses physical strength.
His confidence collapses.
His body no longer responds the way it once did.
And the woman who promised to walk beside him refuses to reduce his manhood to his sexual performance.
She remains his companion.
She speaks with tenderness.
She protects his dignity.
She reminds him that he is still her husband, still worthy of affection, still deeply loved.
That is covenantal devotion.
Not because sexual intimacy is irrelevant.
But because the person is greater than any single expression of the relationship.
The deepest test of love is not whether desire exists. It is whether love remains committed to another person's good when desire cannot be fulfilled.
And please understand: couples who struggle with sexual incompatibility, loss of desire, illness, trauma, or intimacy problems are not automatically failures.
Those difficulties deserve compassionate conversation, appropriate professional care, prayer, patience, and mutual effort.
A relationship without sex is not automatically healthier or holier than one with a fulfilling sexual life.
Nor does the presence of sex prove that love is absent.
The question is what governs the relationship.
Is it self-giving love?
Or self-centered appetite?
Because those two can look surprisingly similar at the beginning.
Both can send good-morning messages.
Both can plan romantic dates.
Both can whisper, "I miss you."
Both can produce butterflies.
But time has a way of exposing the difference.
Desire often asks, "What can I experience with you?"
Sacrificial love also asks, "How can I seek your good?"
Desire can be intense.
Love must also learn endurance.
Desire can make promises in the heat of emotion.
Love must practice faithfulness when emotions fluctuate.
And desire, even when genuine, is not strong enough by itself to carry every burden that life will eventually place upon two people.
There will be sickness.
There will be exhaustion.
There will be grief.
There may be pregnancy, childbirth, disability, hormonal changes, emotional struggles, aging, and seasons of separation.
There will be days when one person feels beautiful and days when they cannot bear to look in the mirror.
If a relationship is sustained only by sexual excitement, what happens when ordinary human vulnerability interrupts that excitement?
What happens when the body grows older?
What happens when beauty changes?
What happens when pleasure requires patience?
What happens when love has to become a verb instead of a feeling?
That is where the question becomes impossible to ignore.
Would you still choose the person if the relationship required more giving than receiving?
And before you direct that question toward somebody else, ask it of yourself.
Would you still be gentle?
Would you still listen?
Would you still remain honest?
Would you still honor boundaries?
Would you still invest emotionally?
Would you still pray for their spiritual growth?
Or have you been measuring love by how successfully another person satisfies you?
It is easy to identify selfishness in someone else's heart.
It is much harder to recognize it in our own.
Perhaps you are the one who has been withholding affection to punish your partner.
Perhaps you have treated intimacy as proof of your worth.
Perhaps you have pressured someone because rejection awakens insecurities you have never confronted.
Perhaps you have used sexual attention to keep someone from leaving.
Perhaps you have crossed boundaries you once promised God you would respect.
Or perhaps you have spent years telling yourself that physical closeness could repair emotional distance.
And now you are beginning to realize that two bodies can be close while two hearts remain painfully far apart.
This is where the Gospel must enter the conversation.
Not as a weapon.
Not as another reason to drown in shame.
But as the truth that exposes sin while offering real redemption.
Jesus Christ did not come merely to improve our romantic choices.
He came to save sinners.
He came to reconcile us to God.
He came to deal with the guilt, rebellion, selfishness, and brokenness that reach into every area of human life, including our relationships.
Romans 5:8 declares:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." (KJV)
Look at the order.
Christ did not wait for us to become worthy.
He did not love us because we could offer Him something He lacked.
His love moved toward undeserving sinners in mercy.
At the cross, we see love expressed through costly self-giving.
And in His resurrection, we see the victory of the Savior who offers forgiveness and new life to those who turn to Him in faith.
That does not mean every romantic relationship must continue regardless of betrayal, danger, or abuse.
Jesus' sacrificial love is never an excuse to demand that another person remain exposed to harm.
But His love does expose our selfishness.
It confronts our tendency to use people.
It calls us to repentance.
And it teaches us that real love cannot be reduced to getting what we want.
Ephesians 5:25 tells husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her.
That is a staggering standard.
Not domination.
Not entitlement.
Not manipulation.
Self-giving love.
And Ephesians 5:21 frames the surrounding teaching with a call to mutual submission out of reverence for Christ.
The biblical vision of marriage is not a competition over who gets served.
It is a covenant in which love is shaped by faithfulness, honor, responsibility, and the example of Jesus.
Somebody needs to hear this:
Being sexually desired is not the same as being sacrificially loved.
And somebody else needs to hear this:
Having sexual desire does not make your love impure. What matters is whether that desire is governed by truth, holiness, and genuine care for the other person.
Both truths matter.
We cannot protect biblical purity by pretending that marital sexuality is unimportant.
And we cannot celebrate marital sexuality by pretending that sexual entitlement is biblical.
God's design is wiser than either extreme.
For the unmarried believer, this means chastity and sexual boundaries are not punishments for falling in love.
They are part of honoring God with your body and treating another person as more than an outlet for desire.
First Thessalonians 4:3–5 calls believers to holiness and self-control rather than sexual immorality.
First Corinthians 6:18–20 calls Christians to honor God with their bodies.
Waiting until marriage does not guarantee a happy marriage.
But obedience to God should never be dismissed simply because it requires restraint.
And for those who have already crossed boundaries, the answer is not despair.
The answer is repentance and grace.
You cannot rewrite yesterday by pretending it never happened.
But your past does not have to become your permanent identity.
First John 1:9 teaches that God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse those who confess their sins.
That is not permission to continue carelessly.
It is an invitation to come out of hiding.
To stop making excuses.
To receive forgiveness through Christ.
To begin walking in a different direction.
Maybe your relationship began in compromise.
Maybe you confused lust with love.
Maybe you gave away more of yourself than you intended because you were terrified of being abandoned.
Maybe you are married and have allowed resentment, selfishness, or emotional neglect to poison what was once tender.
Maybe you are single and quietly wondering whether anyone will ever want you for more than your appearance.
There is grace for the repentant.
There is hope for the wounded.
There is wisdom for those willing to listen.
And there is a Savior who is not intimidated by the truth about your life.
Remember the woman at the well in John 4.
Jesus knew the complicated history of her relationships.
He did not need her to pretend.
He brought the truth into the open.
But He also offered her living water.
Her story was not reduced to her relational history.
The conversation pointed beyond her past toward the Messiah standing before her.
And that same chapter records her going back to her community and speaking about Jesus.
A woman whose life contained painful relational complexity became someone who invited others to encounter Christ.
Not because every broken relationship will be restored.
Not because every person who hurt you will return.
Not because repentance guarantees a wedding, reconciliation, or a happy ending on your preferred timeline.
But because Jesus can redeem a human life even when its history contains sin, heartbreak, shame, and regret.
He can teach a selfish person to become more loving.
He can teach a wounded person to recognize healthy boundaries.
He can teach a married couple to rebuild trust where genuine repentance and safety make restoration possible.
He can teach a single believer that loneliness does not cancel worth.
And He can teach all of us that the greatest love we will ever know is not found in another imperfect human being.
It is found in Him.
Perhaps this is why the original question cuts so deeply.
Because beneath the conversation about sex lies another question.
"Am I loved for who I am, or merely for what I can provide?"
That question belongs to the young woman afraid to lose her boyfriend.
It belongs to the husband who feels inadequate after illness.
It belongs to the wife who wonders whether aging will make her undesirable.
It belongs to the single person tired of being treated like a temporary experience.
It belongs to the person who has mistaken attention for commitment.
And it belongs to the Christian who has learned to speak about love without yet learning how to practice it.
But the answer is not to become suspicious of every attraction or to assume that every sexually active married couple lacks spiritual depth.
The answer is to examine the fruit.
Does this relationship produce greater honesty?
Greater patience?
Greater respect?
Greater responsibility?
Greater willingness to serve?
Greater faithfulness to God?
Does it make room for truth even when truth is uncomfortable?
Can you disagree without being threatened?
Can you express a boundary without being punished?
Can you speak about the future without the conversation always returning to physical pleasure?
Can you pray together without using spirituality to avoid difficult conversations?
Can you admit wrongdoing?
Can you forgive without pretending that trust requires no rebuilding?
Can you genuinely enjoy one another's company?
Because someday, the most meaningful moments in a relationship may have nothing to do with sexual intimacy.
They may look like sitting together after a funeral.
Holding hands in a hospital waiting room.
Laughing over an ordinary meal.
Working through a financial crisis.
Praying through uncertainty.
Helping one another through depression, exhaustion, or disappointment.
Choosing honesty when lying would be easier.
Choosing tenderness when frustration would be more convenient.
Choosing faithfulness when life no longer feels romantic.
And there is something profoundly beautiful about a love that can still say:
"I see you."
"I respect you."
"I am here."
"Your dignity matters to me."
"We will face this truth together."
That is the kind of love worth cultivating.
Not a love without desire.
But a love that is bigger than desire.
And if you are reading this beside someone you love, perhaps tonight you should ask a different question.
Not, "Do you still find me attractive?"
But, "What do you value most about who I am?"
Ask what makes them feel respected.
Ask what makes them feel safe.
Ask where you have been selfish.
Ask how you can grow together in Christ.
And then listen.
Not to defend yourself.
Not to win an argument.
But to understand.
For some couples, that conversation may become the beginning of deeper intimacy.
For others, it may uncover problems that require serious attention.
And for someone reading this alone, it may become the moment you stop confusing being pursued with being cherished.
Please do not turn this article into a weapon against your spouse or partner.
Do not send it with the attitude, "See? This proves you are the problem."
Let the Word of God examine your own heart first.
Because the Gospel does not merely expose what other people need to change.
It calls each of us to surrender.
And that includes me.
That includes you.
That includes everyone who has ever said "I love you" while still learning what those words demand.
So here is the question I want you to carry beyond this article.
If physical intimacy were removed from your relationship tomorrow, would the person beside you still experience your patience, kindness, friendship, honor, and commitment?
And would you experience theirs?
Do not rush to answer.
Let it challenge you.
Let it open an honest conversation.
Let it bring hidden selfishness into the light.
And most importantly, let it bring you back to Jesus Christ.
Because the goal is not merely to find someone who loves you well.
It is also to become someone whose love increasingly reflects the character of Christ.
Someone else may need the encouragement that repentance and restoration are possible.
I also want to hear from married couples, singles, and those who are still healing.
Can a relationship remain deeply loving without sex? And what do you believe distinguishes genuine love from mere physical desire?
Speak honestly. Speak respectfully. And remember that behind every comment is a real person with a story you may not know.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should be a matter of willing conviction, not pressure or compulsion.
We want people to be nourished by God's Word, not merely moved by a single article.
Above everything, keep your eyes on Christ.
Do not merely search for a relationship that makes you feel wanted.
Seek to live a life that honors the One who loved us while we were still sinners.
Do not build your identity on your desirability.
Build your life on the truth of the Gospel.
And do not mistake physical closeness for spiritual unity, emotional safety, or covenantal faithfulness.
Because when beauty changes, health falters, emotions fluctuate, and the excitement of the beginning becomes the ordinary work of remaining faithful, the deeper character of love comes into view.
One day, the question may no longer be whether someone still desires your body—but whether they ever learned to cherish the soul standing before them.
